title: Metallic bonding
examples: What are delocalised electrons in a metal?
Why are metals good conductors of electricity?
How are alloys different from pure metals?

explain.say: Today we explore metallic bonding in metals.
In metals, the outer electrons are not fixed to one atom.
These delocalised electrons allow metals to conduct electricity well.

draw.text: Good conductors due to electron sea

explain.say: Metals are also usually malleable and ductile materials.
An alloy is a mixture of two or more metals together.
In everyday life, stainless steel is an alloy used for kitchen sinks.

faq.q: Why do metals conduct electricity so well?
faq.a: Metals conduct electricity because the delocalised electrons can move freely throughout the structure. These mobile electrons carry the electrical charge easily. You might also ask why metals are good conductors, or how delocalised electrons allow current flow.
asks: How do electrons move in metals?

faq.q: What is the difference between a pure metal and an alloy?
faq.a: A pure metal is made of only one type of element, while an alloy mixes two or more different metals. Alloys are often made to improve properties like strength. You could also ask what an alloy is, or how to make a mixture of metals.
asks: Is brass an element or a compound?
What is a mixture of metals called?

faq.a: Most metals are good conductors, but conductivity depends on the specific metal and its bonding structure. Some metals are better conductors than others. You might ask if all metals conduct, or about variations in conductivity.
asks: Do all metals conduct heat too?

faq.a: Delocalised electrons are outer electrons that are not bonded to any single atom. They are free to move throughout the entire structure of the metal. Think of them as a shared, mobile electron sea. You might ask what electrons are in metals, or where electrons are located in metals.
asks: Are the electrons stuck to the atoms?
What is the electron sea model?

faq.a: Malleability is the property that allows a metal to be hammered or pressed into thin sheets. It means the metal can change shape without breaking. Other ways to ask this are 'can it be flattened' or 'is it sheet-like?'
asks: Can metals be hammered into sheets?

facts: Metallic bonding involves a lattice of positive ions.
The outer electrons are shared freely among all ions.
This sea of electrons allows metals to conduct heat and electricity.
An alloy is a mixture, such as brass (copper and zinc).

quiz.say: Which feature is responsible for metals conducting electricity?
quiz.why: The free movement of these electrons allows charge to flow easily.

wrong.1: The ions are fixed in place and do not carry the charge.
wrong.2: The structure holds the ions but does not carry the charge itself.
wrong.3: The bonds are strong but it is the mobile electrons that carry the current.

quiz.say: If you mix copper and tin, what do you create?
quiz.why: An alloy is specifically defined as a mixture of two or more metals.

wrong.0: An element must be pure, containing only one type of atom.
wrong.1: A solution usually involves dissolving a substance in a liquid.
wrong.3: A compound involves a fixed chemical ratio, unlike a simple mix.

quiz.say: A metal that can be drawn into thin wires is described as:
quiz.why: Ductility specifically refers to the ability to be drawn into wires.

wrong.1: Malleability describes being hammered into thin sheets.
wrong.2: Conductivity describes the flow of heat or electricity.
wrong.3: Lustrous describes the shiny appearance of the metal.
